subsection: 3. Urban settlement: site, hierarchy, hinterland and central place theory

notes.b: A town's site is the exact ground it is built on. Towns grew where the land gave an advantage for crossing rivers, trading, defence or getting resources, and Irish towns show each type.
points: Bridging point or ford (a shallow place where a river can be crossed): Dublin, on the Liffey, is the lowest bridging point on the river, so traffic had to cross there.
Route focus, where several roads meet: Athlone, at a crossing of the River Shannon in the centre of Ireland, gathers traffic from many directions.
Island site: Limerick, on King's Island in the Shannon, which gave natural protection from water on all sides.
Sheltered harbour or estuary head (the inner end of a river mouth where it widens to the sea): Waterford, on the Suir estuary, and Galway, at the mouth of the River Corrib, both suit ships.
Defensive sites on a hill, river loop or island, because attackers find them hard to approach, and dry points above wet ground, which are safe to build on.
Resources close to the site, such as water, fish, timber and stone, which settlers need for living and building.
A river confluence (where two rivers join) is another site characteristic.
notes.tip: Site means the ground the town stands on. Give the feature and name the town, for example Limerick on King's Island.

notes.b: Site is the spot itself. Situation is the wider picture: where the town lies in relation to the land and trade around it.
points: Centre of a fertile farming area, so the town can supply goods to farmers and take in their produce.
On a coast facing trade partners, which gives access to sea routes.
At a gap through the uplands (high ground), where routes crossing the high ground are forced to pass through the town.

notes.b: A function is the job a town does for its own people and for the area around it. Knowing the functions lets you describe what a town is for and, later, how that has changed.
points: Residential (people live there), market and retail (buying and selling), and services such as health, education and administration.
Industrial (making goods), port (handling ships and cargo) and transport (road and rail links).
Tourism and recreation, ecclesiastical (to do with the Church) and defence or garrison (soldiers and fortifications).
Commuter (dormitory) towns, where most residents work elsewhere and the town is mainly a place to sleep.
Most towns are multi-functional, which means they carry out several of these functions at once.
notes.tip: Ordinary questions ask you to name an urban area and two of its functions, and to match photographs of buildings to functions such as residential, commercial, transport or religious.

notes.b: Settlements are not all alike. A hierarchy ranks them by size and by the number and range of their functions and services.
points: The ranking runs from hamlet to village, small town, large town, city and capital (primate) city.
There are few large centres and many small ones, so the hierarchy takes the shape of a pyramid.
A place higher in the hierarchy has more functions and services, so it draws people from a wider area.
notes.tip: Be ready to define primate city, as short questions ask for this.

notes.b: Ireland's settlements fit this ranking from one very large capital down to many small villages. These are Census 2022 figures for cities and suburbs, and for towns.
points: Dublin: about 1.26 million people, far above any other city, so it tops the hierarchy.
Regional cities: Cork, about 222,000; Limerick, about 102,000; Galway, about 86,000; Waterford, about 60,000.
Largest towns: Drogheda, about 44,000, which is Ireland's largest town; Dundalk, about 43,000; Swords, about 41,000. Swords is a town in Fingal, not a separate city.
Many smaller county and market towns, and villages. The State's population is about 5.1 million.
notes.tip: Drogheda is Ireland's largest town, while Galway, Limerick, Cork and Waterford are cities. Use the city and suburbs figures as given. Short questions use data on the largest towns and their growth.

notes.b: In some countries one city dwarfs all the others. A primate city is much larger than the second city in the country and dominates its functions.
points: Dublin is a primate city: about six times the size of Cork, the second city.
Causes of Dublin's primacy: its role as capital, its port, its routeway focus (where routes meet), colonial administration (rule by Britain), multinational firms and services.
The rank-size rule, in which the nth city is one nth the size of the largest, does not fit Ireland, because Dublin is far bigger than that rule predicts.
The National Spatial Strategy and the National Planning Framework (government plans) try to balance Dublin's growth with other centres. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal.
notes.tip: Define primate city and give Dublin as the example with its size compared with Cork.

notes.b: Goods and services differ in how often people buy them and how far they will travel for them. This explains why some are in every village and others only in cities.
points: Low-order goods are for convenience, such as bread and newspapers. They are found in every village, are bought often and have a low threshold (few customers are needed to keep the shop open).

High-order goods are comparison goods (shoppers compare before buying) and specialised services, such as jewellers, department stores, hospitals and universities. They have a high threshold, needing many customers, so they are found only in large centres.

notes.b: No town serves only its own residents. The hinterland, also called the sphere of influence, catchment area or umland, is the surrounding area a town serves and draws people from.
points: The size of a hinterland depends on the town's size and functions, on transport, and on competition from nearby centres.
notes.tip: Hinterland can be set as a short definition question.

notes.b: A hinterland has no fixed edge, so geographers find it by collecting evidence of where people come from to use a town.
points: Newspaper circulation areas (where the town's paper is sold).
Bus routes and timetables, which show where services run to and from the town.
Catchments of schools and hospitals, meaning the areas they draw pupils and patients from.
Shop customer surveys and delivery areas.
Commuter flows, the movements of people travelling to work in the town.
Sports club catchments, such as the areas their members come from.

notes.b: Hinterlands are not fixed. They shift as travel and shopping habits change.
points: Hinterlands overlap, because nearby towns compete for the same customers, and they change over time.
Cars, motorways and online shopping widen hinterlands, because people can reach a town from further away.
Bypasses (roads taking traffic around a town) and out-of-town centres change them.
Example: the large hinterland of Galway city across the West.

notes.b: Central place theory tries to explain why settlements of different sizes are spaced the way they are. Walter Christaller, a German geographer, published it in 1933, based on a study of southern Germany.
points: A central place is a settlement providing goods and services to people in its surrounding area.
Threshold is the minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business. It is a number of people.
Range is the maximum distance people will travel to obtain a service. It is a distance.
A service locates where its threshold falls within its range, so it has enough customers and they are prepared to travel to it.
notes.tip: Do not swap threshold and range: threshold is a number of people, range is a distance. Christaller, 1933, southern Germany. Do not credit Burgess or Hoyt.

notes.b: To make the theory work, Christaller imagined an ideal landscape with no differences between places.
points: A flat, uniform (isotropic, the same in every direction) plain, so nothing blocks movement.
An evenly spread population with equal purchasing power, so demand is the same everywhere.
Equal ease of transport in all directions.
Consumers buy at the nearest centre.
No excess profits, so no centre earns more than the others.

notes.b: On such an ideal plain, the theory predicts a regular pattern of centres and market areas.
points: Market areas are hexagonal, because circles overlap or leave gaps and hexagons fit together.
A hierarchy of centres forms: many small, closely spaced low-order centres, and fewer, more widely spaced high-order centres.
Each higher-order centre also supplies all the lower-order goods, so a city has everything a village has.
Nesting (smaller areas fitting inside larger ones): k = 3 is the marketing principle, k = 4 the transport principle and k = 7 the administrative principle.
notes.tip: The predicted market areas are hexagons, not circles. Examiners ask for threshold, range, hierarchy, hexagons, assumptions, evidence and criticisms, with examples.

notes.b: Some real places roughly match the theory, especially where farming land is fairly even and settlements were planned.
points: In parts of the Irish Midlands, market towns serving farming areas are regularly spaced.

The Dutch polder (land reclaimed from water) Noordoostpolder, in the Netherlands, was drained in 1942. Emmeloord was planned as the central town, with ten villages around it, including Marknesse, Ens, Kraggenburg and Bant.
The villages were spaced so that farmers could reach one by bicycle. This gives a planned two-level hierarchy, an almost perfect example of the theory.

notes.b: Real landscapes are not the ideal plain, so the theory has many weaknesses. Each criticism below breaks one of the assumptions or ignores something real.
points: Relief (the shape of the land), rivers and coasts are not uniform, and population is unevenly spread.
Transport routes are linear, not equal in all directions, so some places are easier to reach.
People shop on the way to work or on multi-purpose trips, not always at the nearest centre.
Car ownership, motorways, out-of-town shopping centres and online shopping change ranges and thresholds.
Government decisions, such as county towns and new towns, and history, such as Viking and Norman towns, fix locations.
Dublin's primacy breaks the regular hierarchy.
The theory was designed for market (service) towns, not for industrial, port or tourist towns.

notes.h: Applying central place theory to Ireland
notes.b: Irish settlements can be set against the theory to see how well it fits.
points: Dublin is at the top, the regional cities come next, then county and market towns, then villages.
The Irish hierarchy is broadly hierarchical but distorted by Dublin's primacy and by the coastline.

notes.b: Towns do not keep the same jobs forever. Across Ireland, some functions have faded and others have grown.
points: Defence functions were lost, so walls and garrisons no longer shape towns.
Market and fair functions declined, as marts (livestock markets) and supermarkets took over.
Industrial functions moved from the inner city to the suburbs or closed, so those areas lost jobs.
Services grew, such as offices, tourism, education and health.
Many towns near cities became commuter towns, for example Navan and Naas.
Village services such as the post office, Garda station, pub, shop and school have closed.
notes.tip: Higher questions ask how the functions or services of urban centres change over time, with examples. Ordinary questions ask you to name an urban area and describe how its functions changed.

notes.h: Galway: Norman port and merchant town
notes.b: Galway is the main case study for changing functions. It began as a walled trading port and grew rich on merchant trade before decline set in.
points: Galway was a Norman town founded by the de Burgo family in the 13th century.
It was governed by 14 merchant families, the Tribes of Galway. A royal charter (a grant of rights from the Crown) of 1484 was granted.
Galway traded wine with Spain and France, which made it a merchant town and port.
The Spanish Arch, built in 1584, is a surviving part of the town walls.
Galway surrendered to Cromwellian forces in 1652, and a long decline followed.

notes.b: After its decline, Galway gained new functions in education, high-tech industry, culture and tourism, and became the regional capital of the West.
points: Queen's College Galway was founded in 1845. It is now the University of Galway, renamed in 2022.
Digital Equipment Corporation opened a plant in Galway in 1971 and closed its manufacturing there in 1993.
Galway is now a centre of the medical devices industry, with multinationals such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific.
The National Spatial Strategy of 2002 named Galway a gateway (a centre chosen for growth). The National Planning Framework of 2018 aims for at least 50% growth in Galway by 2040.
Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, jointly with Rijeka, Croatia.
The Galway Arts Festival and the Galway Races at Ballybrit attract visitors, which supports its tourism function.
Galway is the regional capital of the West.
notes.tip: Do not give job numbers for any Galway company.

notes.h: Limerick: walled city and Georgian port
notes.b: Limerick shows a different path: a river-island settlement that became a fortified city and then a trading port.
points: Limerick began as a Viking settlement, from about 922.
King John's Castle was built in the early 13th century on King's Island, the island site in the Shannon.
The Treaty of Limerick was signed in 1691.
Limerick developed as a Georgian commercial port (Georgian means the 18th-century style of planning and building). Its Georgian Newtown Pery dates from the late 18th century.

notes.b: Limerick moved from port and milling to multinational manufacturing, then lost some of that industry and has rebuilt through education, culture and new governance.
points: Limerick became an industrial city based on its port and flour milling.
Later industry linked to the Shannon area brought multinational investment, including the Shannon Free Zone of 1959 and Shannon Airport nearby.
Dell opened in Limerick in 1990. In January 2009 it announced that it would move manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.
The University of Limerick was founded in 1972 as the National Institute for Higher Education and became a university in 1989.
Limerick was Ireland's first National City of Culture, in 2014.
Limerick City and County Councils merged in 2014.
In 2024 Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor.
notes.tip: Do not give job numbers for any Limerick company except the Dell figure.

notes.b: Dublin's functions changed in stages as new roles were added to the old ones.
points: Viking trading port, from 841.
Administrative capital.
Georgian city, with the Wide Streets Commissioners of 1757 (the body that planned wide new streets).
Port and industry.
Services and technology in the Docklands: the International Financial Services Centre (1987), and Google at Grand Canal Dock.
notes.tip: There is more on this in A Core Irish Region.

notes.h: A market town becoming a commuter town
notes.b: Smaller towns change too. A market town near a big city can lose its old role and take on a new one as a home for people who work elsewhere.
points: Market functions, such as the mart and shops serving farmers, decline as the town's population changes.
Services, housing and shops shift to serve commuters who travel to work in a larger city.
Commuter towns of the Greater Dublin Area include Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones.

notes.h: Reasons for the growth of an urban area
notes.b: When asked why an urban area grew, use this checklist and back each reason with a case study such as Galway or Limerick.
points: Site and situation: a bridging point, island, estuary or harbour.
Route focus and port: the town gathers traffic from roads, rivers or the sea.
Administrative role: a national capital, a regional capital or a merged council.
Industry and multinationals: manufacturing and foreign investment.
Services and education: universities and hospitals.
Tourism and culture.
Government policy: national gateways and growth targets, as in the National Spatial Strategy and National Planning Framework.
In-migration: people moving in for work and study.
notes.tip: Ordinary questions ask for the reasons for the growth of an urban area in Ireland, and why towns develop near ports. Use named examples.

keyTerms.definition: The ground a town is built on, such as a bridging point, island, estuary or defensive hill.
The position of a town relative to the farming area, coast, routes and uplands around it.
The ranking of settlements by size and by the number and range of their functions and services.
A city much larger than the second city in its country, dominant in its functions.
The surrounding area a town serves and draws people from.
A settlement that provides goods and services to people in its surrounding area.
The minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business.
The maximum distance people will travel to obtain a service.
Goods bought often and found in every village, such as bread and newspapers.
Comparison goods and specialised services found only in large centres.
A town whose residents travel out to work, and whose services increasingly serve commuters.

questions.prompt: Examine central place theory with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Walter Christaller published central place theory in 1933, based on a study of southern Germany. A central place provides goods and services to the people of its surrounding area. A service locates where its threshold, the minimum number of customers needed, falls within its range, the maximum distance people will travel. The theory assumes a flat, uniform plain, an evenly spread population with equal purchasing power, equal ease of transport in all directions, that consumers use the nearest centre, and no excess profits. It predicts hexagonal market areas, because hexagons fit together with no gaps, and a hierarchy of centres: many small, closely spaced low-order centres, and fewer, more widely spaced high-order centres. Each higher-order centre supplies all the lower-order goods. Nesting follows k = 3 for the marketing principle, k = 4 for the transport principle and k = 7 for the administrative principle. Evidence: market towns serving farming areas are regularly spaced in parts of the Irish Midlands, and the Dutch polder Noordoostpolder, drained in 1942, has Emmeloord as its central town with ten villages around it, spaced so farmers could reach one by bicycle. Applied to Ireland, Dublin sits at the top, the regional cities come next, then county and market towns, then villages. Limitations: relief, rivers and coasts are not uniform, and population is unevenly spread. Transport routes are linear. People shop on multi-purpose trips, not always at the nearest centre. Motorways, out-of-town shopping centres and online shopping change ranges and thresholds. Government decisions and history, such as Viking and Norman towns, fix locations. Dublin's primacy breaks the regular hierarchy, and the theory was designed for market towns, not for industrial, port or tourist towns.

questions.prompt: Examine how the functions of an urban centre have changed over time, with reference to one example you have studied.
questions.model: Galway. It was a Norman town founded by the de Burgo family in the 13th century, governed by 14 merchant families, the Tribes of Galway, and given a royal charter in 1484. Its walled port traded wine with Spain and France, and the Spanish Arch of 1584 is a surviving part of the town walls. Galway surrendered to Cromwellian forces in 1652, and a long decline followed. Queen's College Galway was founded in 1845, and is now the University of Galway, renamed in 2022. Digital Equipment Corporation opened a plant in Galway in 1971 and closed its manufacturing there in 1993. Galway is now a centre of the medical devices industry, with multinationals such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific. The National Spatial Strategy of 2002 named Galway a gateway. The National Planning Framework of 2018 aims for at least 50% growth in Galway by 2040. Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, jointly with Rijeka, Croatia. Its functions have moved from trade and defence, to education, high-tech manufacturing, tourism and culture, and it is the regional capital of the West.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one urban area you have studied. (ii) Name two of its functions. (iii) Describe and explain how its functions have changed over time.
questions.model: (i) Limerick. (ii) Two functions: port and industry, and education. (iii) Limerick began as a Viking settlement. King John's Castle was built in the early 13th century on King's Island, and the town was walled. The Treaty of Limerick was signed in 1691. In the late 18th century it developed as a Georgian commercial port, with Newtown Pery laid out. It became an industrial city based on its port and flour milling, and later multinational investment linked to the Shannon area brought new industry. The decline of older industry followed, and Dell announced in January 2009 that it would move manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs. The University of Limerick was founded in 1972 and became a university in 1989. Limerick was Ireland's first National City of Culture in 2014, and in 2024 it elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor. The functions moved from port and military defence, through industry, to education, culture and regeneration.
